newsitem.title: UK: British budget is likely to target consumers.
newsitem.headline: British budget is likely to target consumers.

text.p: Consumers in Britain are unlikely to escape unscathed when Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown presents a special budget on Wednesday, financial analysts increasingly believe.

Most analysts argued last week that the budget would raise an extra 4.0 billion stg ($6.7 billion) largely from the corporate sector, but press comment now predicts Brown has decided he must also tackle the ebullient private sector to guard against an unsustainable boom.

If such forecasts are proved right, they will go some way towards alleviating fears in the financial markets that British official interest rates will be raised in July for the third time in as many months.

Without higher taxes, the Bank of England is likely to try to calm the consumer sector, fevered by payments totalling 30 billion stg from building society mergers and flotations, by increasing rates from the current 6.5 percent.

Strong economic data and a survey showing house prices rising in June by an annual rate of 11.0 percent, their strongest since the third quarter of 1989, now suggest Brown will target the private sector, analysts said.

The Observer, a left-leaning Sunday newspaper which has had a number of accurate "leaks" since the May 1 election, said Brown would make a double attack on the housing market to prevent inflationary pressures there from contaminating the economy as a whole.
It said Brown would reduce a current tax break on mortgage interest payments (MIRAS) from 15 percent to 10 percent at a cost to Britain's 10 million homeowners of up to 10 stg per month.

Earlier newspaper reports had suggested Prime Minister Tony Blair had vetoed a reduction in MIRAS, fearing it would look as if his Labour Party, which returned to power in May after 18 years in opposition, was reneging on the spirit of its election pledge not to raise income tax.

The Observer said Brown was also likely to increase stamp duty on property transactions at the top end of the market to around 2.0 percent. Stamp duty is now levied at a flat rate of one percent on homes worth 60,000 stg or more.
But, in an attempt to balance these measures, Brown will also increase spending on social housing by releasing the proceeds of council house sales, the paper reported.

Two economic think tanks -- Cambridge econometrics and Oxford economic forecasting -- warned that interest rates would have to rise, giving another boost to the already robust pound, unless Brown took a firm line.
Without a tight budget, the British economy would move into an unsustainable boom, Cambridge econometrics said in its latest edition of Industry and the British economy.
It assumed that Brown would impose a tight fiscal policy and this would cause sterling's average rate against the Deutschemark to fall to 2.55 in 1998 and 2.35 in 1999.
Unless he increased taxes, "sterling could remain at around 2.80 Deutschemarks for another year or more," it said.

Oxford forecasting said that without higher taxes and with only a modest overshoot of the current tight spending plans the government would not reach by 2001-02 its own golden rule of borrowing only to finance investment -- some one percent of GDP.

The budget was also expected to introduce environmentally-friendly measures such as cutting value-added tax (VAT) on loft insulation to five percent from eight percent, bringing it into line with a reduction in VAT on domestic fuel due to be announced.

But the corporate sector was also in Brown's sights and Advance Corporation Tax (ACT), which gives a tax break to shareholders, was likely to be reduced from 20 percent. Analysts were split on whether it would be cut to 15 percent or 10 percent.
A reduction would be aimed both at saving the government money and at encouraging firms to invest their profits rather than distributing them in dividends.
Brown will also unveil a long-awaited windfall tax on privatised utilities which is now expected to garner around 5.0 billion stg.
